nature-econ-551.title: Endogenous growth: explaining progress from the inside
nature-econ-551.text: Older growth models, such as the one in {{ref:nature-eecon-204}}, left long-run growth to technical progress they could not explain. Endogenous growth theory arose in the mid-1980s to fill that gap. It explains growth from inside the economy, through increasing returns, the gains from experience in {{ref:nature-clim-207}}, or firms' research and development. Knowledge spillovers, a kind of positive externality, keep returns to capital from falling to zero. So the long-run growth rate depends on policy, such as subsidies for research or education. Critics dispute its explanatory power, and ecological economists fault its neglect of energy and materials.

nature-econ-568.title: The unpaid work the national accounts ignore
nature-econ-568.text: An Australian study put the value of unpaid work, such as household work, at about 50% of GDP. None of it appears in the national accounts or in GDP, which may distort the picture they give. Unpaid housework falls outside the SNA production boundary, the line that decides what counts as production. Feminist economists such as Marilyn Waring and Nancy Folbre call this biased, noting that GDP still imputes a rent for owner-occupied homes. They say it hides how much market production depends on non-market labour. Statisticians question whether valuing such work is feasible.

nature-econ-505.title: The circular flow ignores the energy that drives it
nature-econ-505.text: The textbook circular flow has a hidden assumption. It implies the economy runs like a perpetual motion machine, something the {{ref:nature-eecon-118}} rule out. No economy can recycle its own waste without new energy, so it must operate as a subsystem of a larger ecosystem. In this critique, the economy depends on a one-way {{ref:nature-eecon-136}} of matter and energy from the environment. Concentrated, useful matter and energy enter from natural capital such as solar energy, oil wells, fisheries and mines. They leave as dispersed, useless waste, a change physicists describe with {{ref:nature-eecon-109}}. Because these inputs and the capacity to absorb waste are finite, there is a sustainable limit to the economy's growth. For this reason, {{ref:nature-eecon-059}} replaces the simple circular flow with a diagram that includes solar energy and the natural inputs and services it sustains.

nature-econ-537.title: Imputed rent: the rent homeowners pay themselves
nature-econ-537.text: Homeowners who live in their own houses pay no rent, yet national accounts record one for them. The imputed rent of owner-occupied housing is the market rent owner-occupiers would receive if they rented their homes out. National accounts add it to value added, and so to GDP. The idea is that a dwelling provides its owner with a service, whether or not anyone pays for it. Critics call this addition largely fictitious, since nearly all owner-occupiers do not actually rent out their homes.

nature-econ-498.title: Is national income a good measure of welfare?
nature-econ-498.text: Cleaning up an oil spill adds to GDP, while the lost well-being from fouled beaches goes unmeasured. A paid nanny's income counts in GDP, but a parent's unpaid childcare does not. Such cases raise the question of how well GDP per person reflects people's welfare. It is not useless: countries with higher GDP may also score higher on other welfare measures, such as life expectancy. Still, alternatives exist, including {{ref:nature-acct-003}}, indexes of sustainable economic welfare and genuine progress, and a sustainable version of national income.

nature-econ-552.title: Putting nature into models of the whole economy
nature-econ-552.text: In 1865, Jevons's book The Coal Question made an unsettling argument: in a growing economy, productivity gains could speed up resource scarcity. Economists have since tried to build nature into macroeconomic models, especially growth models, by adding resource scarcity and {{ref:nature-hist-007}}. During the oil crises of the 1970s, Stiglitz and Solow added resources that run out to growth models, asking whether living standards could keep rising. The 2006 {{ref:nature-clim-268}} gave the first comprehensive analysis of global economic damage from projected changes in climate. Integrated assessment models, pioneered by {{ref:nature-hist-050}} and covered in {{ref:nature-clim-248}}, are now widely used to estimate regional and global climate damages under different policies. Such models treat land, water and energy as inputs to production. Early work by {{ref:nature-hist-040}} replaced the familiar picture of money circling between households and firms with one driven by solar energy. How to count environmental goods and services in national accounts is still debated.
